topic: Discrete Convolutions: The Art of Sliding and Combining
target_audience: Undergraduate engineering or computer science students

sections.title: The Big Idea: The 'Echo' Effect
lecture_lines: Convolution describes how one function modifies another.
Imagine a signal passing through a system with memory.
A Cyber-Frog jumps on a quiet digital pond.
Each splash creates ripples that fade over time.
Total state equals the sum of all past ripples.
animations: Title 'Discrete Convolution' in white (#FFFFFF) fades in at center; background is #000000.
A yellow circle (#FFFF00) representing a 'Cyber-Frog' jumps on a blue horizontal line, leaving a white vertical spike.
Three blue bars (#0000FF) of decreasing height appear at the jump site, representing an 'echo' or ripple.
The frog jumps twice more, creating two more sets of blue bars that overlap with the first set.
The overlapping bars are replaced by a single green profile (#00FF00) representing the sum of all ripples at each point.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Signals as Sequences
lecture_lines: Discrete signals are ordered sequences of numbers.
Input x[n] meets an impulse response h[n].
Visualize these sequences as bars on a graph.
animations: A sequence of blue vertical bars (#0000FF) labeled 'Input x[n]' appears on a horizontal axis.
A smaller sequence of orange bars (#FFA500) labeled 'Kernel h[n]' appears next to it.
Both signals are aligned on a common integer axis with white labels (#FFFFFF).

sections.title: The Mechanics: Flip, Slide, Multiply, Sum
lecture_lines: First, flip the kernel horizontally to prepare.
Slide the kernel across the input signal step-by-step.
Multiply overlapping values at each discrete position.
Sum these products to find the output point.
Repeat across all steps for the full result.
animations: The mathematical formula (x * h)[n] = sum(x[k] * h[n-k]) appears in white (#FFFFFF) at the top.
The orange kernel h[n] is mirrored horizontally (flipped) relative to its center.
The flipped kernel slides from left to right along the axis towards the blue input signal.
Overlapping regions of the signals flash yellow (#FFFF00) and multiplication products are shown.
A new cyan bar (#00FFFF) appears in the output sequence for each sliding step's sum.

sections.title: Application 1: Smoothing the Noise
lecture_lines: Convolution can smooth out noisy, jittery sensor data.
A uniform kernel computes a local moving average.
This creates fluid movement from raw, shaky inputs.
animations: A jagged red line (#FF0000) representing noisy sensor data scrolls across the screen.
A white semi-transparent box (#FFFFFF) slides over the red line, representing the smoothing window.
A smooth green line (#00FF00) is drawn in the path of the box, showing the filtered result.

sections.title: Application 2: Feature Detection in 2D
lecture_lines: Convolution extends naturally to two-dimensional image grids.
A small kernel slides over pixels to find patterns.
Specialized kernels highlight edges in digital images.
This helps self-driving cars identify highway lane markings.
Feature maps extract essential information for the computer.
animations: A 5x5 grid of gray squares (#888888) appears, representing a digital image.
A 3x3 yellow frame (#FFFF00) containing the Sobel matrix slides across the grid.
Pixels in the grid that form a vertical edge are highlighted in white (#FFFFFF).
An output grid shows bright spots only where edges were detected.
The scene transitions to a simple visual of a car identifying lane lines (#FFFFFF).

sections.title: Summary: The Universal Tool
lecture_lines: Convolution is essentially a weighted local average.
It powers modern breakthroughs in Convolutional Neural Networks.
From signals to AI, convolution extracts deep meaning.
animations: Icons for audio, imaging, and AI appear in cyan (#00FFFF) around a central kernel.
The text 'Weighted Local Average' (#FFFFFF) expands to fill the center of the screen.
The screen fades to black with final text: 'Convolution: The Language of Systems'.
